newsitem.title: USA: U.S. West spot power down, warm weather cuts usage.
newsitem.headline: U.S. West spot power down, warm weather cuts usage.

text.p: Spot power prices in the western U.S. slid further as warmer weather reduced demand and hydroelectric power supplies remained abundant, trade sources said Tuesday.
"Demand seems to be falling off because of the temperatures, also the hydro numbers look strong," said one trader.
He added that relatively smooth operations at thermal and nuclear generating plants in the West helped soften spot market prices.
The 1,158 megawatt (MW) WNP-2 nuclear unit in Washington was expected to remain at 68 percent power through the end of the week amid work to correct an adjustable speed drive problem.

A 350 MW unit at the Comanche coal-fired plant in Colorado was expected to be shut until January 29, while curtailed units at the Colstrip coal-fired plant in Montana were expected to be back on line this week.

According to Weather Services Corp, the Northwest will see average temperatures and rain in coastal areas through mid-week. The Southwest was expected to see scattered rain with below normal temperatures early in the week rising to above normal by the end of the week.
Wednesday firm, peak electricity at the California-Oregon border (COB) was quoted $14.00-15.00 per megawatt hour (MWh), down from $15.00-18.00 for Tuesday.
Firm, peak power at Mid-Columbia (Mid-C) fell to $13.00-15.00, while off-peak was at $9.50-10.50.
Firm, peak Palo Verde (PV) electricity was quoted $15.00-17.00, down from $16.00-19.00.
Off-peak PV was quoted $10.00-11.00 per MWh.
Next-day firm, peak prices at Four Corners were quoted $15.00-16.00, while off-peak was at $9.00-11.00.
February COB was last quoted $12.90-$13.15, while PV was at $15.00-$15.35.
Power for second-quarter delivery at COB was last quoted near $11.00, while PV was at $14.65-$14.70.
